competencies: Appreciates families and the vocabulary related to family relationships and descriptions
Understands the home environment and the roles of the people at home
Understands knowledge concerning practices of growing crops, plants and making food
Appreciates knowledge concerning practices of animal rearing
Understands language related to should be able to basic hygiene
Knows about growth and development in adolescents and the management of peer pressure
Uses language related to wellbeing in the school environment
Understands appropriate behaviour and language used in public places
Appreciates traditions and rituals of baptism and naming
Understands different occupations, professions and careers and their related terminologies
Communicates apporriately about games and sports including traditional games
Uses language related to wildlife and cultural heritage sites
Appreciates own identity and expresses fundamental knowledge of symbols, taboos and “if beliefs”
Uses language related to wealth creation
Uses appropriate language related to environmental management
Knows language related the importance of water
Appreciates own identity and origin
Appreciates traditional practices of initiation, marriage and funeral rites
Appreciates own cultural values and morals
Understands vocabulary related to systems of governance
Appreciates individual rights
values: Honesty; uphold and defend the truth at all times
Justice and fairness in dealing with others
Integrity; moral uprightness and sound character

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates families and the vocabulary related to family relationships and descriptions.
learning_outcomes: pronounce, listen to, read and write the Local Language (k, s).
differentiate between Local Language alphabet and the English alphabet (u).
use vowel length (s).
describe family genealogy and relationships (k, u).
write numerals (k, s, gs)
write days of the week, months of the year and dates (k, u, s)
write time (k, u).
welcome, greet and bid farewell using appropriate vocabulary (words) while observing time, number, gender and age of people (k, v).
use gestures that accompany greeting to express respect, age difference/similarity and so on (s, gs).
write informal letters (k, s, gs).
use riddles related to family (k, v).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learner illustrates the English language alphabet on the board.
the teacher guides the learner to identify, list and pronounce letters of the local language alphabet from a given text.
learner populates the generated list of sounds/letters with relevant examples of words from the text studied.
learner constructs additional words outside the given text that contain specific sounds.
teacher engages learner in a spelling exercise by dictating specific words especially those with common confusing sounds such as dh and th, ng and ŋ and those with diacritic marks.
teacher brainstorms with learners about members in their families.
teacher draws an example of a family tree on the board.
through discussion, teacher asks learner to study a family tree chart and asks them to state any reasons for its arrangement.
teacher then wraps up the discussion.
using the given example of a family in (2), learners draw family trees reflecting their own immediate family genealogies.
teacher asks learners in groups to read a short text of a half-page containing numbers 1-20 in words.
teacher asks learners to write numbers 1-20 in figures and words.
teacher explains common rules observed in writing numbers beyond 20 in words.
using the principles learnt, learners write numbers beyond 20 in words (21-1,000,000)
teacher asks learners to mention their position of birth in family.
teacher asks learners to line up and mention their positions in the line.
teacher provides learners with flashcards containing ordinal numbers 1-20.
using examples in flashcards, learners write ordinal numbers 21-1000.
teacher asks learners what day of the week it is.
learners read aloud a poem about days of the week and corresponding activities.
teacher asks learners to write days of the week and their activities from the poem.
teacher presents learners with a table of months of the year in the local language.
learners match months of the year in English and the local language.

teacher demonstrates how to write dates in a local language e.g. 03/12/1454. Ka adek dwe marapar g’aryo oro ma gana achiel pyer’apar dingwen gi pyer’abich g’angwen (Dhopadhola); Nga isatu omwezi gwa Namuwawuzo, mu mwaka lukumi bina ataanu n’ena(Lusoga); Eraasi auni olap loka Orara okaru loka ilukumit akwata aungon akaisiakany aungon (Ateso).
teacher points key prepositions, conjunctions and punctuations involved in writing date e.g. ‘on’.
teacher asks learners to write their personal birthdays and those of three family members.
teacher asks learners to divide and name parts of the day: dawn, morning, noon, afternoon, evening and night in the local language.
teacher guides learner to group times of the day into morning, afternoon, evening and night e.g. 12am-11am (morning), 12pm-3pm (afternoon), 4pm-7pm (evening), 8pm-11pm (night).

through group discussion, the teacher asks learners to write equivalents of specific terms such as am, pm, second, minute, hour, time, half-past, quarter-past or quarter-to, break, lunch, dinner, supper, etc. in the local language.
teacher illustrates to learners how to write given time in the local language in words or figures e.g. 10:15am (Sawa angwen gi dakika apar g’abich m’odikini); saawa inhha ne dakiika ikumi na itanu.
teacher asks learners to pair up and greet one another.
teacher asks one learner to greet a group of learners.
learner greets the teacher.
teacher asks learners to talk about/explain what rules they followed while greeting in scenarios 1-3.
teacher clarifies or sums up rules involved in greeting (time, number, gender, title, and age).
teacher guides learners to construct a greeting dialogue.
teacher asks learners to discuss and demonstrate how they would greet peers, in-laws, women, men, and elders.
teacher engages learners to critique the greeting demonstrations and clarifies on some gestures.
teacher asks learners to comment on the greeting gestures from other cultures vis-a-viz their own.
teacher asks learners to mention types of letters they know.
teacher asks learners to identify examples of people to whom informal letters can be written.
teacher demonstrates on the board or presents a text example of an informal letter.
teacher asks learners to study example in 3 and identify parts of the letter.
teacher guides learners to write their own letters to a family member, friend or relative.
teacher begins the lesson by giving examples of riddles and learners respond.
teacher groups learners and tasks them to write ten riddles.
learners share their collections with the rest of the class.
after sharing, teacher asks learners to suggest importance of riddles.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: compares Local Language and English language alphabets.
spells words from a dictation.
transcribes words recorded in an electronic device.
tabulates words according to vowel length e.g. bana vs baana, baba vs baaba, etc.
writes a greeting dialogue with two responses for each time variation, that is, morning, afternoon and evening.
responds to questions from an audio or audio-visual recorded greeting dialogue.
writes given figures in the local language using words e.g. 14,579.
writes a letter to a relative.
poses and responds to five riddles related to family.
draws an extended family tree.

practicals.title: Family Tree
practicals.description_verbatim: learners draw family trees reflecting their own immediate family genealogies.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: as an individual project, teacher may ask learners to generate a larger relational tree of their families and clans.
project_requirements.deliverables_verbatim: larger relational tree of their families and clans

suggested_uses: use recorded episodes to support development of listening and speaking skills.

topics.core_competency: The learner understands the home environment and the roles of the people at home.
learning_outcomes: tell roles of different people at home (k, u).
appreciate members of the family for carrying out their roles efficiently using appropriate vocabulary (v, a).
appreciate the values of lullabies at home (k, v).
name objects found at home in singular and plural (k, u).
identify how some traditional objects, crafts and wears are made (k, u).
explain the importance of domestic objects and wears (k, v).
appreciate traditional fashion and style (k, v)
appreciate the taboos related to the misuse of some of the objects at home (v, a).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher probes learner to name titles of different people at home.
through a discussion, the teacher asks earners to describe the roles of people at home.
in their groups learners generate lists of common words related to roles played in a home.
learners engage in a conversation using common words used in a family.
teacher provides a text on appreciation.
learners identify the words/ language used in appreciation
learners share life examples/ personal experiences of appreciation/gratitude.
in groups, learners explain the purpose/benefits of appreciation and effects of ingratitude.
learner writes a letter of appreciation to a family member for help received.
teacher probes learners to mention various songs sung in their community and their purpose.
the teacher picks out a lullaby and explains what it is.
the learners sing the lullabies they know from their communities.
in their groups learners compose lullabies.
leaners present their composed lullabies.
teacher provides a text with plural and singular forms of objects found at home.
learners identify objects they have at their homes.
the learners generate a table of singular and plural forms of objects at home
teacher guides learners to identify some traditional objects, crafts or wears and describe how they are made.
teacher sums-up the process of making any given traditional object, craft or wear e.g. mortar/pestle, sieve, rope, mat, footwear or backcloth.
learners write a half-page composition describing how any chosen traditional object, wear or craft is made.
in groups, learners discuss the importance of any traditional object or wear.
learners present their group’s finding in a plenary.
teacher guides learners to appreciate the concept of moral and physical beauty.

with vivid examples, teacher guides learners to discover aspects of moral beauty of a person in a traditional setting (honesty, appropriate language, respect of rule of law and order, respect for elders, hard work, etc.)
in groups, learners discuss aspects of physical beauty of a person in a traditional setting (decency, adornment, grooming, tooth extraction, body size, traditional dress codes, etc.)
using specific examples, teacher guides learners to understand the meaning of ‘taboo’.
in groups, learners identify and discuss the purpose of taboos associated with misuse of some objects found in a home.
learners share their findings in a plenary.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: debates on topics related to the family such as: ‘Mother is more important to the family than Father.’
writes the singular and plural of objects found at home.
writes a letter of apology or of gratitude to a family member.
writes a lullaby, rehearses it and discusses its importance.
makes a traditional object such as a banana fibre ball or skipping rope.
writes a one-page essay describing how one traditional object is made.
debates on traditional beauty vs modern beauty.
picks a role model from each side of beauty and explain why they admire them.

explains the rationale of at least five taboos associated with misuse of some traditional objects/crafts/wares. e.g Not sitting on the mortar is for hygiene purposes i.e. the mortar is used for preparing food and therefore should be kept clean/not be contaminated.
identifies at least five proverbs associated with the taboos on misuse of those objects /crafts/wares.
writes a short essay on the roles of people at home (100-150 words).

practicals.title: Making Traditional Object
practicals.description_verbatim: makes a traditional object such as a banana fibre ball or skipping rope.

suggested_uses: use the Internet to obtain images or digital camera to take pictures of the objects in a home to support class discussion.
Use a computer to prepare a list of tribes and their cultural dress codes (where applicable).

themes.theme_title: 1.3 Crops, Plants and Foods in Our Area

topic_metadata.topic_title: 1.3 Crops, Plants and Foods in Our Area

topics.core_competency: The learner understands knowledge concerning practices of growing crops, plants and making food.
learning_outcomes: categorise food crops, non-food crops and wild plants and understand their importance to the family/ community (k, u, v).
differentiate seasons of the year and understand their impact on agricultural activities (k, u, v).
use appropriate vocabulary in the Local Language during planting and harvesting (k).
study the taboos related to crop growing, harvesting and seasons and how they affect the crops (k, v, a).
identify the techniques used in improving crop yields (k, v).
describe the process of food preparation (k, v).
describe ways of preserving and storing crops and food (k, v).
describe a food menu (k, u).
use a dictionary (k, u, s, gs).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher groups learners and asks them to identify examples of food crops, non-food crops and wild plants in the community.
teacher guides learners to discuss the importance of crops and wild plants to the community.
learners write one-page composition describing the importance of crops.
learners study a text on different seasons and their impact on agricultural activities.
learners identify seasons mentioned in the text and their respective activities.
learners identify impacts of the season on the activities.
teacher guides learners to understand how their community categorises seasons e.g. by weather patterns or activity.
learners in their groups discuss and identify activities carried out in particular seasons and why.
learners share experiences of how they grow and harvest any crop at home or school.
teacher provides a descriptive text on the process of growing and harvesting any chosen crop.
teacher guides learners to brainstorm on certain terms and processes as indicated in the text.
learners write a one-page description of the steps involved in growing and harvesting any crop.
teacher introduces the concept of taboos by asking learners to brainstorm the purposes of rules and regulations at school.
teacher asks learners to relate school rules and regulations to taboos involved in growing and harvesting crops.
teacher asks learners to research and report on taboos related to growing and harvesting crops in their communities.
teacher asks learners to talk about what crops were grown in their communities in their previous season and whether the yields were good or not.
teacher asks learners to explain what could have caused better or poor yields.
in groups, learners discuss methods of improving crop yields.
in their groups, teacher asks to categorise methods into traditional and modern practices.
teacher asks learners to mention various types of foods, sauces and beverages prepared at their homes.
teacher groups learners and allocates them different types of foods and asks them to describe the process involved in preparing such a food.
learners make a report on (2) above.
teacher asks learners to brainstorm on what takes place at mealtime.
in groups, teacher asks learners to identify examples of good and bad manners portrayed while having a meal.
teacher asks learners to identify the methods of food preservation or storage.
in groups, teacher tasks learners to identify the types of food and how they can be preserved or stored.
in groups, teacher provides learners with manilla papers and asks them to draw any type of food preservation or storage system known to them.
in their groups, learners present their work.
learners brainstorm on what foods, sauces and beverages they often have for a meal at home.
the class visits any local restaurant to appreciate how a food menu is prepared.
while in the field, learners take notes.
in groups, teacher asks learners to write a food menu using their field notes.
in groups, teacher provides learners with a dictionary or photocopies and guides them to locate certain words.
learners pronounce words they have located and use them to construct different sentences.
in their groups, learners display their sentences on charts.
with specific examples, teacher illustrates the meanings of synonyms, antonyms and homophones.
learners complete assignments on synonyms, antonyms and homophones.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: reads and answers questions from a comprehension passage on effects of seasonal changes on crops.
mentions five advantages of growing crops to the family/ community.
holds a debate on different topics related to agriculture such as modern vs traditional techniques of farming, advantages and disadvantages of farming, etc.
writes two taboos related to crops.
uses a graphic organiser/ template to communicate the process of preparing a favourite food.
prepares and acts a skit to educate people about table manners etiquette.
correctly pronounces particular words on a given list.
explains meanings of given words.
re-arranges given words in alphabetical order.
using minimal pairs differentiates meanings of homophones.

practicals.title: Drawing Storage System
practicals.description_verbatim: draw any type of food preservation or storage system known to them.

suggested_uses: use a Word processor to prepare a food menu.
use a digital camera to take pictures of local crops.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates knowledge concerning practices of animal rearing.
learning_outcomes: name domestic animals, birds, their products and understand their importance (k, u, v).
differentiate punctuation marks and their functions (k, u).
explain taboos related to domestic animals and poultry (v, a).
identify the symptoms and traditional ways of treating some common sicknesses that affect animals (k, u, v, a).
know animal rights (k, u, v).
explain the relationship between animals and different communities in Uganda (k, u, v, a).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher asks learners to mention animals and birds they know.
in their groups, the learners generate a list of domestic animals, birds, their young ones and shelter.
the learners share lists.
learners discuss the importance of domestic animals and poultry.
learners research and report on ways in which domestic animals and birds contribute to livelihoods.
by way of tabulation, learners identify animals/birds and their young ones.
teacher provides a varied-punctuated text for the learner to read.
the learner identifies the different punctuation marks used in the text.
learner writes them in their local language.
learner compares them with those in the standard orthography.
leaners discuss the use/importance of each of them.
learner punctuates a given text.
teacher asks learners to identify taboos related to domestic animals and poultry.
in two groups: one for domestic animals and the second for poultry, learners discuss the taboos.
each group reports their findings.
learner writes an essay on the taboos.
teacher provides a text on animal/bird diseases.
learner describes symptoms of different diseases.
learner generates a table on animal and poultry diseases and their traditional treatment.
teacher provides a text on animal rights for learners to study.
learners identify two animal and poultry rights.
learners share their opinions/feelings on animal rights.
in their groups, learners write a composition on animal rights.
teacher guides learners to brainstorm on animals found in their communities.
learners discuss the uses of animals in different communities.
learners describe agricultural activities relating to animal rearing.
learners debate on the relationship between animals and people.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: reads/listens to a text on a topic related to health issues of animals and/or birds and answers questions.
writes a letter to his/her father informing him of the state of the animals or poultry at home.
writes a composition on the importance of domestic animals and poultry (half-page).
discusses the importance of observing the rights of animals.
reads a one-paragraph passage on the importance of domestic animals and punctuates it correctly.
fills a table with names of five animals, their young ones and shelter.
debates on topics related to birds and animals e.g. “poultry keeping is better than animal rearing.”

suggested_uses: use a Word processor to generate a list of domestic animals, their young ones and shelter.
use the Internet to obtain images of domestic animals.
generate a table on animal and poultry diseases and their treatment.

topics.core_competency: The learner understands language related to should be able to basic hygiene.
learning_outcomes: use words related to hygiene and how it is maintained at personal and community level (k, u, v, gs).
name internal and external parts of the body that are prone to disease due to poor hygiene (k, u).
translate words and short sentences (k, s).
maintain personal hygiene and proper sanitation (gs).
explain how to prevent various diseases using traditional approaches and modern methods k, u).
compose and write simple songs and poems (s).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners study a text on personal and community hygiene.
teacher guides learners to identify words related to hygiene from the text.
learners brainstorm the meanings of words identified.
learners use the words identified to construct sentences.
teacher groups learners, provides them with charts and asks them to draw and label the human body.
in their groups, learners identify parts of the body that are prone to disease.
learners identify different diseases that affect internal and external parts of the human body.
in groups, teacher provides learners with translated text on parts of the body and human diseases.
in their groups, learners translate short sentences related to parts of the body and human diseases into the local language.
teacher assesses learners’ work.
teacher identifies some simple songs from different languages about health and tasks learners to translate them.
learners brainstorm the different ways on how proper hygiene and sanitation are maintained.
learners discuss advantages of maintaining proper hygiene and dangers of poor hygiene.
in groups, teacher asks learners to recap various human diseases.
in their groups, learners suggest ways of preventing and treating diseases mentioned.
teacher guides learners to categorise the prevention and treatments into traditional and modern methods.
learners study sample poems/songs.
teacher recites a poem and learners sing a song along with teacher.
in groups, learners compose poems and songs about hygiene.
learners sing the songs or perform their poems.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: discusses the causes of diseases related to poor hygiene in their community.
suggests ways of preventing common diseases in the community.
draws and labels the human body.
matches six diseases related to hygiene and the body parts they attack.
writes four paragraphs about keeping their bodies and environment clean, observing the rules of orthography.
composes simple songs and poems.

practicals.title: Drawing Human Body
practicals.description_verbatim: draw and label the human body.

suggested_uses: use electronic devices to record plays/songs/poems in a Local Language.
use mobile thermometer, stethoscope and sphygmomanometer (Blood Pressure Machine) for measuring one’s body temperature, breathing and pressure.

topics.core_competency: The learner knows about growth and development in adolescents and the management of peer pressure.
learning_outcomes: describe changes experienced during adolescence and their effects on the person (k, u).
use verbs (k, u).
identify challenges of peer pressures and how to manage them (k, u).
know the impacts of peer pressure on young people in decision-making. (k, u, v/a)
identify dangers of drug abuse, e.g. alcohol, marijuana, “weed”, cigarettes (k, u).
use appropriate vocabulary to overcome challenges associated with peer influence (k, u, s, gs).
explain what a diary is (k, u).
state why keeping a diary is important (k, u, v)
mention what to keep in a diary and how (k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: using prior knowledge, teacher guides learners to brainstorm on what adolescence is and the age at which it begins.
in groups, learners outline the biological changes experienced during adolescence.
learners discuss the effects of those changes on girls and boys in their groups.
teacher guides learners to identify specific terms related to adolescence and their equivalents in their local language.
learners translate a text on adolescence from English to their local language (quarter page).
teacher guides learners to understand a verb.
in their groups, learners list the verbs they know and use them to construct sentences.
the leaners identify and use key verbs that describe biological changes during adolescence.
the teacher probes learners to identify who peers are citing examples.
in their groups, leaners discuss challenges in managing relationships among young people.
leaners perform a dialogue on persuasion and resistance to peer pressure.
in groups, learners share the impact of peer pressure.
the teacher prompts learners to give their personal judgements on the impact of peer pressure.
learners read and respond to texts relating to peer influence.
learners write their personal experience on the effects of peer pressure.
the teacher guides leaners to brainstorm on what drug abuse is.
in their groups, the leaners name drugs that are abused locally and their effects.
the leaners answer questions from a dictated passage about drug abuse.
in groups, leaners write a short article for the local media explaining dangers of drug abuse.
the teacher groups leaners and provides them with passages/pictures relating to peer influence for them to interpret.
learners translate a passage about drug abuse from English into local language.
through a role-play, learners express their views clearly and coherently.
through question and answer, teacher guides leaners to brainstorm on what a diary is.
in their groups, learners study a sample diary provided by the teacher.
learners discuss the features/format of a diary.
in their groups, the leaners brainstorm on the type of information to keep in a diary.
the learners brainstorm on the advantages and disadvantages of keeping a diary.
the teacher probes leaners to identify how people in the past kept their information.
the teacher tasks learners to fill out a hypothetical diary for a week using appropriate tense.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: listens to a conversation and notes down perspectives on peer influence.
describes orally their experiences in managing peer pressure.
discusses the dangers of drug abuse.
writes a letter to a friend advising them against drug abuse giving reasons.
lists five verbs related to growth, maturation and relationships.
writes a persuasive dialogue on how one can resist peer pressure.
reads a passage on dangers of drug abuse and answers the questions accordingly.
translates a one-paragraph text on drug abuse or peer influence.
writes one-passage essay on the effects of drug abuse.
writes an expository essay on the advantages and disadvantage of keeping a diary.
debates on why diary is not popular.
designs a diary for a particular period such as a school term, etc.
writes an argumentative composition comparing traditional ways to the modern ways of storing information.

suggested_uses: use electronic devices to record information in the diary.
watch a movie on the effects of good/bad peer influence.

topics.core_competency: The learner uses language related to wellbeing in the school environment.
learning_outcomes: describe the school environment (k, u).
write a descriptive composition (k, u, s).
differentiate types of schools (k, u).
use adverbs (k, u, s).
appreciate school routines (v, a).
explain what news is (k, u).
identify various sources of news and how to extract it (k, u).
present news on different platforms (s).
fill in forms, identity cards and so on (s, gs).
understand the importance of school rules (k, u).
identify the types and causes of strikes in schools (k, u).
describe an incident witnessed in a public place (k, u, s).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher probes learners to brainstorm on what environment is.
in their groups, learners list ten things found at school.
learners name five different categories of people found at school.
learners name different places at school.
the teacher tasks learners to draw a map of their school and locate different places on it.
teacher provides a sample descriptive text.
teacher guides learners to identify elements/ principles/characteristics of a descriptive text from the sample.
learners write a composition of 150 words describing the school environment.
through question and answer, the teacher guides the learner to outline the types of schools that are common in Uganda.
in their groups learners analyse what differentiates the schools/ different curricula.
teacher probes leaners to explain what an adverb is.
leaners identify adverbs from a text provided by the teacher.
leaners construct sentences using given adverbs.
teacher probes leaners to narrate what happens in a normal school day.
in groups, learners discuss different programmes that take place in the school and their rationale.
the learners interpret school schedules/lists and tables, for example a timetable.
teacher guides leaners to draw a class routine chart.
learners are tasked to fill in important events on a class calendar.
teacher probes learners to explain what news is.
in their groups learners identify the different ways in which news is delivered in their community.
the learners mention/talk about their favourite news presenters on both radio/tv and the time of broadcast.
in their groups, learners discuss qualities/characteristics of a good news reader/format of a good news article.
learners listen to news on a radio broadcast.
learners read a news article extracted from one of the local dailies.
as project work the learners are tasked to gather news for the school newspaper/newsletter.
teacher groups learners and asks them to study sample forms and other official documents.
teacher guides learners to analyse and extract key information from the sample forms and other official documents.
in their groups, the learners fill in the forms and other official documents as guided by the teacher.
teacher probes learners to explain what “rules” are.
in groups teacher guides learners to reflect and discuss examples of rules in their family/community.
learners outline rules in their school in their groups.
teachers brainstorm with learners the importance of family/social rules.
in groups, learners discuss the importance of school rules.
learners present the outcomes of their discussion in a plenary.
teachers and learners brainstorm the meaning of strikes.
teacher guides learners to identify types of strikes. (sit-down, hunger strikes, demonstrations, laydown tools).
in groups, learners study a text/article on strikes and identify the causes.
in their groups, learners analyse the causes of strikes in schools.
learners discuss advantages and disadvantages of strikes at school in their groups.
learners suggest how strikes can be avoided.
in groups, learners prepare a persuasive speech to discourage others from striking.
learners deliver their speeches in a plenary.
teacher provides an oral or written account of a real or imaginary incident witnessed in a local centre, for instance, a fistfight, an accident or a theft for learners to study.
in plenary leaners vividly describe an incident, such as a fight, or an accident they witnessed.
learners produce well-structured pieces of writing of one page, which clearly express an argument or specific viewpoint using a wide range of language related to public places.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: draws a sketch map of a school showing the locations of different places.
identifies adverbs from a given text.
writes a brief essay explaining why they like the news presenter they have selected.
presents news (relating to school and community) to the class/school assembly.
writes a persuasive speech discouraging others from striking.
debates on the impacts of strikes.
assumes the role of a school representative and gives a speech on the causes and impacts of school strikes.

practicals.title: Drawing School Map
practicals.description_verbatim: draw a map of their school and locate different places on it.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: as project work the learners are tasked to gather news for the school newspaper/newsletter.

suggested_uses: use a camera to take pictures of the school environment.
use the Internet to study about school strikes, and obtain images about objects and areas around the school to scupper class discussions.
use a computer to prepare a news item.

topics.core_competency: The learner understands appropriate behaviour and language used in public places.
learning_outcomes: acquire appropriate vocabulary concerning public places such as shops, markets and hospitals (k, u).
explain activities pertaining to buying and selling (k, u, v, a, gs).
write a dialogue (s).
use tenses (k, u, s).
describe activities in hospitals (as public places) using appropriate vocabulary and punctuation (k, u).
develop customer care skills and marketing skills (gs).
recognise dress codes for different public places (v, a, gs).

suggested_learning_activities.description: the teacher asks learners to study a map extract of a local trading centre or town.
teacher guides learners to interpret the map extract and guides them to identify specific public places.
leaners read a text provided by the teacher on public places.
in groups, learners identify specific words used in different public places.
learners construct sentences using the words they have identified (in 4 above).
learners make a visit to a nearby trading centre and interact with the community.
teacher guides learners to interpret public signs and notices.
learners roleplay a bargain for a commodity during a transaction in a market.
in groups, learners identify the appropriate negotiation and persuasion skills, phrases and sentences in marketing or buying a commodity.
teacher groups learners and tasks them to act a transaction.
learners study a sample dialogue in groups.
teacher guides learners to write a conversation of one page (8-10 pairs) on an activity between a buyer and seller carried out in a market/shop.
learners act a telephone conversation as the teacher observes.
learners respond to an exercise on a telephone conversation.
teacher provides learners with a sample text with varied tenses.
teacher guides the learners to identify all the different tenses in the text and their tense markers.
learners write sentences in different tenses. (present, past and future).
teacher groups learners and tasks them to identify, draw and name five objects found in hospital.
in groups, learners name five categories of people found in the hospital and their roles.
teacher pairs learners and tasks them to engage in a telephone conversation between a patient and doctor.
teacher guides learners as they demonstrate conversation etiquette.
teacher brainstorms with learners on what attracts them to buy certain items on the market.
in groups, learners share their personal experiences.
teacher provides a text containing different products for learners to choose an item/product and try to convince customer to buy it.
in pairs, learners role play/dramatise number (3) above.
learners write an advert to market an item/product as guided by the teacher.
learners make an exhibition of the products.
respond to news on a market survey and answer questions related to it.
listen to a radio advert on an item.
teacher guides learners to identify different professions that have specific dress codes.
learners brainstorm on the rationale for the dress codes.
learners describe how a person working in any one public building/location should dress.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: identifies types of public places and describes activities carried out in them.
writes a composition of 100-150 words about an experience in any one public place.
role-plays the interaction between a buyer and seller in a marketplace.
writes a conversation between a doctor and patient of about one page.
listens and responds to a radio advert on a product and answers related questions (the advert can be recorded or read to the class).
writes a composition of 200 words giving a first or second-hand account of an incident.

suggested_uses: use a camera to take pictures of public places, local signposts and images to support classroom discussions.
use an online Geographical Information System (GIS) to obtain an insight in the plan, map interpretation and location.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates traditions and rituals of baptism and naming.
learning_outcomes: explain how (ways in which) people acquire names (k, u, v, a).
use key vocabulary applicable to baptismal/ aqeeqah and naming activities. (u, k)
state the importance of rituals associated with baptismal/ aqeeqah and naming ceremonies. (u, v/a)
understand how nouns and verbs are formed.
identify the values of bearing a name that reflects ones’ origin. (u, v, a)
identify songs related to naming (k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners talk about the meanings of their names.
teacher brainstorms with learners on how and when children are named.
in groups, learners describe different ways in which children/people acquire names.
in their groups, learners explain situations that induce people to give names to their children.
teacher guides learners to list and categorise names according to situations of naming.
in their groups learners identify surnames with masculine and feminine equivalents. (e.g. Ngobi vs Nangobi- Lusoga, Oketcho vs Nyaketcho– Dhopadhola)
as project work, learners collect twenty surnames and investigate their meanings and origins.
learners study a text on baptism.
teacher guides learners to identify and discuss key vocabularies used in the text.
learners use vocabularies identified to construct sentences (god-father, god-mother, overcoming Satan, sprinkling water, candle, etc.)
teacher guides learners to describe a naming ceremony they ever attended.
learners identify the different rituals associated with naming.
in their groups, learners analyse the importance of the rituals identified above.
teacher guides leaners to identify five proverbs associated with naming.
learners recap the meanings of noun and verb with examples.
using appropriate examples, teacher demonstrates to learners how nouns and verbs are formed.
in groups, learners study a text on noun and verb formation and respond to questions on the text.
teacher gives a list of names from different ethnic groups, religions and clans and asks for learners’ opinion.
learners brainstorm on the values/importance of names.
teacher guides learners to point out at least two levels of identity associated with names.
teacher sings a song related to naming.
teacher asks learners to explain the subject and purpose of the song.
in groups learners identify other examples of naming songs and perform them.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: reads a text and responds to questions on baptism /aqeeqah and naming.
states five names of personal significance (e.g. names of members of his/her family) and describes the circumstances surrounding their meanings/ origins.
states a name that he/she would love to give to his/her child and gives reasons.
compiles a list of proverbs associated with names in his/her culture.
collects and writes various naming/ baptismal songs in his/her culture.
composes and performs a song related to naming.

project_requirements.project_scope_verbatim: learners collect twenty surnames and investigate their meanings and origins.
project_requirements.deliverables_verbatim: list of twenty surnames with meanings and origins

suggested_uses: listen or watch recordings of traditional naming ceremonies.

topics.core_competency: The learner understands different occupations, professions and careers and their related terminologies.
learning_outcomes: identify the the various professions in the world of work (k, u).
identify terminologies used in the different professions and occupations (k, u).
identify different places of work for the various professions/occupations (k, u).
appreciate the dress code for the different professions (v, a, gs).
write a CV (s, gs)
write an application letter (s, gs).
write an apology letter (s, gs)
describe what comedy is (k).
explain characteristics of comedy (k).
state the merits and demerits of comedy (k).
use personal pronouns (k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher asks leaners to identify the various professions/careers in their communities and schools.
learners talk about their career interests and why.
teacher guides learners to identify other professions and occupations in the world of work.
individually learners write a one-page essay explaining their career interests.
learners mention titles of people working in different professions/occupations.
teacher guides learners to derive professions from verbs.
learners identify professionals and what they do e.g. teacher-teaches, a doctor-dragonises/prescribes /treats, a lawyer-defends/prosecutes suspects, driver-drives,etc.
teacher identifies terminologies and tasks learners to use them to construct sentences.
teacher guides learners mention the equipment and tools used in different occupations.
learners mention the work places of their relatives and friends.
teacher provides learners with a text on different professions and workplaces. (e.g. mechanic- garage, judge-court, shopkeeper – shop, teacher-school, doctor-hospital, etc.
learners answer questions on the text.
teacher provides leaners with a chart having samples of different dress codes and asks them to match them with corresponding professions.
in groups, learners describe dress codes of other professionals they know.
learners discuss reasons for the different dress codes in their groups.
teacher guides learners on how to present information about themselves.
learners talk about themselves - bringing out necessary information. (random selection).
teacher provides a sample cv for learners to study.
learners identify aspects of a cv basing on the sample (format).
individually learners write personal cvs.
learners study a sample application letter.
from the sample letter, teacher asks learners to identify parts of an application letter (format).
teacher provides a sample job advert to which he/she responds with learners.
in an exercise, learners write an application letter
teacher asks learners whether they have ever wronged any one.
then asks them to share how they respond when they have done something wrong.
a role-play in which a learner is apologising to a superior (e.g. a parent, teacher, prefect, priest, police officer etc.)
learners study a sample apology letter identifying key parts.
in an exercise learners write an apology.
teacher brainstorms with learners on what comedy is and who comedians are.
learners describe any comedian they know.
learners identify other persons they consider to be comedians in their community, school, media and beyond explaining why.
in groups teacher guides learners to suggest what makes a comedian comic.
learners brainstorm on why people perform comedy.

in their groups, learners discuss the benefit of comedy in society, e.g. entertainment, stress reliever, excitement, income generation, talent expo/development, mirror what happens in society, advocacy.
in a plenary, learners present their responses to (6) above.
teacher guides learners to recap their understanding of pronouns.
using examples, teacher illustrates to learners what personal pronouns are (singular and plural).
teacher guides learners on how to construct sentences using personal pronouns.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: answers comprehension questions about a given passage on professions/ occupations.
writes a composition explaining his/her profession/ occupation interest.
fills in a table on the different professions and their respective places of work.
translates texts on different professions.
debates on topics related to places of work e.g. “uniforms should be abolished at places of work.”
writes an application letter for a job attaching a c.v.
presents a comic skit on a topic/issue selected from the learners’ suggestions.
writes a composition about a comedy s/he enjoy and the lessons learnt.
writes a composition on the merits and demerits of comedy to society.
matches tools and equipment with their respective professions/ occupations in a matching exercise.
draws a table to show personal pronouns and their plural forms.
writes a report about a tour to a place of work highlighting activities taking place there.

suggested_uses: use a project to display to various dress codes for different professions.
project a comedy.
use e-mail, social media, SMS or wikis to share information and collaborate with one another.

topics.core_competency: The learner communicates apporriately about games and sports including traditional games
learning_outcomes: identify games and sports played in the locality (k, u).
describe the importance of games and sports (k).
differentiate between modern and traditional forms of games and sports (k, u, v).
use possessive and demonstrative pronouns (k, u)
explain disadvantages of games that involve gambling and why the law prohibits them (v, a)
use vocabulary applicable to games and sports (k, u, s).
plan an event (s, gs).
write a biography (s).
explain what leisure is (k, u).
state forms of traditional and modern leisure activities (k, v, a)
describe the merits and demerits of leisure (k, v, a)
write an argumentative composition (k , s)

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners brainstorm on the games and sports played in their school and community.
teacher guides learners to identify the rules or process/steps involved in playing a particular game or sport.
learners write a one-page composition describing a game or sport they have ever watched or played.
in groups, learners discuss benefits of games and sports giving relevant examples.
in a plenary learners present their opinions.
learners brainstorm on modern and traditional games and sports.
teacher guides leaners to identify terminologies used in different games and sports.
learners use terminologies identified to construct sentences.
with relevant examples, teacher guides learners to understand possessive and demonstrative pronouns.
learners study a text and identify possessive and demonstrative pronouns.
learners use two possessive and demonstrative pronouns to construct sentences.
with relevant examples learners brainstorm on the meaning of gambling.
learners identify different games that involve gambling.
in groups learners discuss advantages and disadvantages of gambling citing relevant examples.
learner narrate their own/other peoples’ luck or bitter experiences in gambling.
using a sample text, teacher guides learners to identify key vocabulary from the text.
using the above example, learners generate key vocabularies for different games and sports.
in groups, learners act the role of a sports committee and plan for an event.
teacher guides learners to draw a budget for a one day sports event.
learners study a sample biography.
teacher guides learners to understand the format of a biography.
learners study and extract key information from the biography of a sports hero/heroine.
learners write a short biography of a real or imaginary sporting hero (male or female).
learners brainstorm the meaning of leisure.
in groups, learners identify traditional and modern leisure activities.
in a debate, learners discuss merits and demerits of leisure.
learners study an exemplar argumentative composition.
teacher guides learners to identify aspects or principles of an argumentative composition.
learners respond/do an exercise on an argumentative composition of two pages e.g. “sports have done more harm than good in our society”; “watching premier league should be banned in schools”, etc.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: writes a composition describing a favourite game or sport in about one hundred words.
discusses the benefits of games and sports in small groups and make a class report on their findings.
in groups, designs a poster warning against involvement in gambling.
identifies possessive and demonstrative pronouns from a given text.
conducts a debate on the topic: ‘traditional games and sports are better than modern ones’.
groups exchange reports for review and comment.
reads extract of different aspects of leisure and responds to questions appropriately.

practicals.title: Designing a Poster
practicals.description_verbatim: designs a poster warning against involvement in gambling.

suggested_uses: use a camera or internet to obtain images of traditional and modern games.
use a computer software to prepare an invitation/ poster for a sporting event.

topics.core_competency: The learner uses language related to wildlife and cultural heritage sites.
learning_outcomes: articulate tourism vocabularies (k, u).
identify names of wildlife found in zoos and parks (k, u).
understand noun classes 1-4 (where applicable) (u).
appreciate the importance of cultural heritage sites and objects (v, a).
describe the importance and challenges of wildlife in parks and zoos (v, a).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners study a sample text on tourism.
teacher guides learners to identify and discuss tourism vocabularies in the text.
learners translate those vocabularies in local language and use them to construct sentences.
teacher asks learners to share their experiences of wildlife they have seen in their communities, zoos and parks.
in groups, learners generate names of animals and birds found in zoos and parks.
with the aid of ICT/tv/media, teacher guides learners to identify more wild animals and birds.
in their groups learners write at least five similes related to wildlife.
in their groups, leaners compose a poem about local wildlife.
in plenary, learners recite their poems.
using appropriate examples teacher guides learners to recap the understanding of nouns.
with relevant examples teacher guides learners to understand noun classes 1-4.
in groups, learners generate at least five nouns in classes 1-4.

with relevant examples, learners brainstorm on objects and sites they consider culturally significant in their locality e.g. trees, water bodies, hills, mountains and sacred places such as places of worship and sacrifice.
teacher guides learners to discuss the significance of the above sites and objects.
teacher guides learners to discuss the importance of wildlife to community and nation.
in groups, learners share the difficulties faced in keeping domestic animals.
further, learners brainstorm on the challenges of conserving wildlife.

teacher guides learners to write an argumentative composition on the merits and demerits of wildlife conservation e.g. “wildlife has done more harm than good to our society”; “game parks and zoos should be turned into farmland”, etc.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: compiles a list of common tourism vocabularies borrowing from other learning areas such as social studies.
role-plays the function of a tour guide and explains to tourists about the birds in uganda.
writes a composition of 200-250 words about the importance of cultural sites.
writes and illustrates a notice to prohibit the local population from encroaching on national parks.
writes an animal story (fable) of 200-250 words.
debates on ideas and information obtained from various sources including the media on wildlife conservation and cultural heritage issues.
writes an apology letter for a job you he/she is unable to take.

suggested_uses: project pictures of various tourist sites.
use a camera to take pictures of animals and birds or use the Internet to obtain images of animals and birds found in the environment.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates own identity and expresses fundamental knowledge of symbols, taboos and “if beliefs”.
learning_outcomes: name clans found in their tribe (k).
identify clans and their totems (k, u, v)
understand noun classes 5-10 (where applicable) (k, u).
write an invitation letter (s, gs).
talk about ‘If’ beliefs (v, a)

suggested_learning_activities.description: with relevant examples, teacher guides learners to understand the meaning of clan.
in groups, learners identify clans in their ethnic groups and discuss their origins.
in a plenary, learners make an oral presentation on the origin of any one clan.
teacher guides learners to identify and classify names according to clans.
with relevant examples, teacher guides learners to understand the meaning of a totem.
in groups, learners identify their clans and totems.
with the aid of a chart or board, teacher wraps up and provides further guidance on clans and their totems.
teacher guides learners to brainstorm the importance of totems.
using appropriate examples, teacher guides learners to recap their understanding of noun classes.
with relevant examples, teacher guides learners to understand noun classes 5-10.
in groups, learners generate at least five nouns in classes 5-10.
teacher tasks learners to identify events that require invitations.
learners study a sample invitation letter.
using the above example, teacher guides learners to understand the format of an invitation letter.
in their groups, learners write an invitation letter for a graduation party.
teacher explains the meaning of ‘if’ beliefs using vivid examples.
in groups, learners generate a list of ‘if’ beliefs.

teacher asks learners to justify the validity of ‘if’ beliefs e.g. is it true that “if your palms itches, you are likely to receive money?” “if an owl sings at night, death will occur?” “if one sits on a mortar, they develop hydrocele”.
from the above discussion, teacher guides learners to understand rationales underlying ‘if’ beliefs.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: in a tree diagram or any other graphic form, illustrates the origin of his/her clan.
discusses any possible totems found in the clan.
identifies four “if beliefs” and interprets them.
translates/ interprets from local language into English a passage that talks about the origin of his/her tribe.
reads a passage and identifies nouns belonging to classes 5-10.
writes a letter inviting people to a clan function.

suggested_uses: use presentation software to prepare a photo story about any clan.
Type an invitation.
Use a computer to draw a list of clans and their totems.

topics.core_competency: The learner uses language related to wealth creation.
learning_outcomes: understand what wealth is (u).
explain how wealth can be created or generated (k, u).
use adjectives to talk about wealth creation (k, u).
explain how wealth can be productively or unproductively used (k, u).
identify proverbs, poems, songs, similes and idioms related to wealth creation and poverty (k, v).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher brainstorms with learners the meaning of wealth.
in groups, learners cite different forms of wealth.
teacher asks learners to declare what they consider personal wealth.
after declaring examples of personal wealth, learners share personal experiences on how they acquired such wealth.
in groups, learners discuss socially acceptable and unacceptable ways, activities or practices of wealth creation.
in plenary, each group presents outcomes of their discussion in (3) above.
teacher invites a resource person or uses “pakasa” extract of the new vision to share personal experience on wealth creation.
teacher guides learners to recap their understanding of adjectives.
learners study a text with adjectives on wealth creation.
teacher guides learners to identify adjectives from the text.
individually, learners list ten (10) adjectives and use them to construct sentences.
learners share personal/family experiences on how they productively or misused wealth.
in groups, learners brainstorm on how wealth can be used productively or misused.

learners debate or write compositions on various topics relating to productive and unproductive use of wealth e.g. “the love of money is the root cause of all evil”; “with money all things are possible”; “a wealthy person does not need people”.
learners brainstorm on any proverbs, similes, poems, songs and idioms they know.
in groups, learners identify and explain proverbs, similes and metaphors related to wealth and poverty.
learners compose and perform songs and poems related to wealth and poverty.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: discusses in small groups the disadvantages of wealth mismanagement and poverty.
explains in 200-250 words the various ways of creating wealth using appropriate vocabulary.
role-plays on the impacts of wealth mismanagement.
describes a rich person who can be considered as a role model.
identifies any adjectives in a given text.
conducts research on proverbs, poems, similes and idioms related to wealth, riches and poverty.

suggested_uses: use a mobile phone to share a business for wealth creation.
listen to or watch audio-visual recordings to learn about wealth creation.
use a photo to explain wealth creation.

topics.core_competency: The learner uses appropriate language related to environmental management.
learning_outcomes: mention the components of nature that make up the environment (k,).
explain causes of environmental degradation (k, u, gs).
identify measures that can be taken to reduce environmental degradation (s, gs).
write or make an announcement (s).
use prepositions and postpositions (k, u).
compose poems and creative prose about environmental degradation and conservation (s).
explain key vocabulary and their meanings related to environment(k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners recap the meaning of environment.
learners brainstorm on the components of nature that make the environment.
learners study and interpret maps and data about climate in Uganda and changes to historical climate patterns and summarise them in writing.
learners translate half-page text on environment.
teacher takes learners to observe evidence of environmental degradation from a nearby site e.g. excess soil erosion, garbage dumping sites, deforestation, industrial complex, etc.
learners share their discoveries from the field visit in plenary randomly.
learners study a text and answer questions on the causes of environmental degradation.
teacher engages learners to discuss a local environmental problem and propose actions to be taken to prevent a disaster.
in groups, learners identify general causes and effects of environmental degradation and suggest possible remedies.
learners act the role of environment officer to deliver a speech on environmental awareness.
learners plant at least two trees in the school or community to curb environmental degradation and write a notice explaining why he/she planted them.
in groups, learners study a sample announcement.
using the above sample, teacher guides learners to identify elements/format of an announcement.
in groups, learners prepare an announcement on a given event for radio, poster, assembly, newspaper or any other media.
using relevant examples, teacher explains to learners the meaning of preposition/postposition.
learners study a text and identify prepositions and postpositions.
learners generate further examples of prepositions/postpositions and use them to construct sentences.
learners write an announcement for a local radio on prevention of environmental degradation.
learners study an imaginative or creative text on environmental degradation and conservation.
using the above text, teacher guides learners to understand/appreciate elements of imaginative/creative writing.
learners compose a poem/imaginative prose piece about environmental degradation and conservation.

In groups, learners study a text with key vocabulary related to environment such as degradation, conservation, reclamation, afforestation, deforestation, soil erosion and terracing and translate it into their local language.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: conducts research on environmental terminologies, for instance, from SST Learning Area and translates them in the Local Language.
reads and responds to questions on texts on environment/ climate change.
studies various media about the causes of environmental degradation and writes a short article for the school magazine giving the dangers of environmental degradation.
shows cooperation by persuading a group to agree on key points in a discussion on degradation/ disaster areas.
in a group, discusses how the environment can be conserved, using a local example.
writes a composition of 200-250 words on the dangers of environmental degradation using appropriate vocabulary and punctuation.

debates the following scenario arguing for or against the move: the village members are planning to expel an old man from the village because he is said to be the cause of a long dry spell in the area.
watches films or reads texts regarding climate change and disasters and summarises them in 80- 100 words.
reads and responds to a poem on environment.
writes a short poem/story based on his/her personal response to this topic.

practicals.title: Tree Planting
practicals.description_verbatim: learners plant at least two trees in the school or community to curb environmental degradation

suggested_uses: use the Internet to obtain images of climate changes.

topics.core_competency: The learner knows language related the importance of water.
learning_outcomes: study a comprehension passage on the sources of safe or unsafe water (s).
summarise a passage (s).
explain the importance of water (gs).
translate large texts (s).
describe common water creatures using adjectives (k).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners brainstorm on local sources of safe and unsafe water.
learners study a sample comprehension text.
teacher guides learners to understand the principles of studying a comprehension.
learners read a comprehension passage on how to maintain water safety and respond to questions. (the passage should entail traditional and modern ways of water preservation).
teacher explains to learners the meaning of summary writing.
using a sample, teacher guides learners to understand the principles of summary writing.
learners study a passage on dangers of drinking unsafe water and summarise it.
learners identify importance or uses of water.
for every use in (1) above, learners identify the verb used.
using (1) and (2) above, learners suggest a title and compose a poem on it.
learners study a sample text and translate it (quarter-page).
teacher randomly assesses learner’s work and guides them to understand the principles of translation.
using the above principles, learners translate a large text (half-page) on waterborne diseases.
learners identify aquatic creatures.
learners write two sentences describing each creature.
using the assignment in (2) above, teacher asks learners to identify adjectives used.
teacher clarifies on adjectives of size, quality, quantity, base, comparative and superlative (for example a hippopotamus is the biggest aquatic animal but with the smallest tail (superlative)).

suggested_assessment_activities.description: summarises a passage on a disease caused by drinking unsafe water (acquisition, symptoms, treatment)
carries out an interview in the community to collect views on their sources of water.

in a group simulation, acts as a local leader and addresses the people in his/her village on ways of preventing and treating waterborne diseases. the other learners ask questions and discuss the issues.
uses verbs to construct five sentences describing the importance of water.
composes and performs a poem of 80-100 words about water creatures.

suggested_uses: use the Internet to obtain images of water creatures.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates own identity and origin.
learning_outcomes: trace his/her origin (k, u, v).
apply conjunctions for different purposes (k).
describe some myths about the origin of his/her tribe/clan and their significance (k, v, a).
use interjections and idiophones (k, u).
appreciate the settlement patterns in relation to other tribes (v, a).
appreciate cultures from other tribes and clans (v, a).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher randomly selects learners to narrate stories of their origin.
learners study a sample text of the origin of any clan/ethnic group.
teacher guides learners to understand characteristics of a good narrative or principles of story writing.
using principles learnt in (3), learners write a story of 400-500 words narrating their origin.
learners recap their understanding of conjunctions.
learners identify the conjunctions used in the story above (competence a).
learners outline all conjunctions they know and use them to construct sentences.
using relevant examples teacher explains the meaning of a myth to learners.
in groups, learners discuss myths about the origin of their clan/tribe, chants and their significance.
in plenary learners present their findings and recite their chants.
using relevant examples teacher explains the meanings of interjections and idiophones to the learners.
in groups, learners study a sample text and identify interjections and idiophones.
learners further discuss the significance of interjections and idiophones.
teacher outlines interjections and idiophones on the board and tasks learners to use them in sentences.
teacher brainstorms with learners on the meaning of migration.
learners study maps/diagrams showing migration patterns.
in groups, learners discuss the causes of migration.
teacher tasks learners to write about one significant migration, its causes and its route.
teacher probes learners to talk about their cultural practices and values.
Learners discuss the differences and similarities in cultures/values from other tribes/clans.
in groups, learners identify culture practices/values they admire from other ethnic groups and discuss why.
learners role play a cultural practice.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: gives an oral or written account of his/her tribe’s migration.
writes an essay or composition on the causes of migrations.
writes five clans and their totems in his/her tribe.
demonstrates a clan chant.
in groups, dramatises the origin of a tribe or clan.

suggested_uses: use audio-visual recordings to demonstrate a story of origin of your tribe.

themes.theme_title: 4.2 Traditional Ceremonies: Initiation, Marriage and Funeral Rites

topic_metadata.topic_title: 4.2 Traditional Ceremonies: Initiation, Marriage and Funeral Rites

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates traditional practices of initiation, marriage and funeral rites.
learning_outcomes: explain types and purposes of marriages, funeral rites and initiations (where applicable) (k, v, a).
describe types of traditional songs, dances and poems (k, v, a).
explain the processes involved in identifying marriage partners (k, v, a).
take minutes (k, s).
describe activities done during funeral rites (chants, singing, etc.) (k, v, a).
use specialised vocabulary associated with marriage, funeral rites and initiation (k, s).
identify proverbs and idioms related to marriage, initiations and funeral rites (k, u, v).
describe chants and incantations and their significance (where applicable) (k, s, v, a).
write a will (k, s).
conjugate verbs (where applicable) (k).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher probes learners to talk about their cultural practices and values.
learners share on the differences and similarities in cultures/values from other tribes/clans.
in groups, learners identify culture practices/values they admire from other ethnic groups and discuss why.
learners role play a cultural practice.
teacher tasks learners to identify songs that suit different ceremonies such as initiation/ wedding/traditional marriage ceremony.

in groups, learners compose and sing songs and poems on traditional ceremonies like initiation wedding/traditional marriage, folksong, traditional anthem, religious/sacred ceremonies, funeral, naming, work, traditional slogans (“omubala”-Lusoga and Luganda), and lullabies.
in plenary different groups of learners perform any form of traditional dance e.g. initiation/post-initiation, funeral, twin, fertility, general, courtship, war, marriage, etc. where applicable.
teacher tasks learners to draw and name instruments and costumes used for different traditional dances in groups.
learners discuss the importance of songs, dances and poems.
learners share an experience of a recent marriage in their home/community and explain how the couple met.
learners study a text on courtship and marriage.
in groups learners brainstorm on the stages involved in getting a marriage partner.
teacher tasks learners to discuss the different ways in which a partner can be identified.
in groups, learners compare the tradition and modern ways in which people identify partners.
using an example of a marriage ceremony known to them, learners mention gifts given during marriage ceremonies and their significance.
learner writes an imaginative or real life story about a marriage ceremony he/she has attended.
learners study a sample of minutes of a meeting.
teacher guides learners to understand the format of writing minutes.
learners attend a class meeting and write minutes.
learners share an experience of a recent funeral rite they attended in their community.
learners identify activities and process during funeral rites.
in groups, learners discuss the significance of the activities and practices done during funeral rites.
learners study a text on marriage, funeral rites and initiation and translate it into local language.
teacher identifies key vocabularies and tasks learners to use them to construct sentences.
learners brainstorm on any proverbs and idioms they know.
in groups, learners identify and explain the meanings of proverbs and idioms related to marriage, initiation and funeral rites.
in their groups, learners write a speech for a marriage or funeral ceremony with appropriate use of proverbs and idioms.
in plenary, learners deliver their speeches.
teacher demonstrates to learners an example of a chant or incantation they know.
using the above example, learners identify other examples of chants and incantations.
learners categorise clans and their chants or incantations.
teacher guides learners to brainstorm the significances of chants and incantations.
learners study a sample will.
teacher guides learners to understand the format and content of a will.
learners discuss the significance of a will.
learners write and read a will.
using relevant examples, teacher illustrate the concept of verb conjugation.
teacher identifies verbs and asks learners to conjugate (for example, marry, marries, and marrying).
learners construct sentences using conjugated verbs.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: describes stages involved in a cultural marriage ceremony in a graphic organiser.
describes the traditional ceremonies practised in his/her locality.
describes personal experiences in the form of a letter to a friend.
writes a composition of 250-300 words starting with a proverb.
writes and performs at least one chant or incantation.
generates a will using a given template and someone’s biography.
reads a given text and identifies verb conjugations that have taken place.

suggested_uses: use audio-visual recordings/documentary about funeral rites/ marriage/initiation ceremonies.
use electronic devices to record plays/songs/poems in Local Language about funeral rites/ marriage/initiation ceremonies.

topics.core_competency: The learner appreciates own cultural values and morals.
learning_outcomes: express gratitude/ thanking (v, a, gs).
explain why some personalities are taken as role models in society and appreciate the contributions of such personalities (k, v, a).
identify the forms of dress found in the community (k, v, a).
use verb extensions 4-6 (where applicable) (k, u).
explain corruption and its various forms (k, v, a).
state causes and effects of corruption in society (k, u).
explain how to fight corruption (k, u, gs).
use noun classes 11-14 (where applicable) (k, u).
understand how compound nouns are formed (where applicable) (k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: teacher asks learners to share personal experiences and life examples of appreciation/gratitude.
learners brainstorm on situation that require appreciation and words used.
in groups, learners discuss the purposes of appreciation and the consequences of ingratitude from personal experience.
learners roleplay gestures and words used in expressing/ingratitude from different ethnicities.
learners brainstorm the meaning of role model.
teacher guides learners to identify people they consider role models and why.
in groups, learners discuss the qualities or virtues of role models.
learner writes a composition describing one person he/she considers a role model.
learners brainstorm on dress codes for people of different age groups in their communities and give their opinion.
considering different ages groups, learners discuss what they consider acceptable or unacceptable dress code.
learners discuss the values of decent dressing e.g. respect, honesty, integrity.
teacher moderates the discussion and wraps up clarifying on pertinent issues.
teacher guides learners to recap their understanding of verb conjugations.
using relevant examples, teacher illustrates verb conjugations 4-6 (for example, kola, kolera, kolakola, kolerera, koleka, kolesa)
in an exercise, teacher identifies verbs and asks learners to conjugate verbs in levels 4-6.
teacher guides learners to understand the meaning of corruption.
in groups, learners identify forms/examples of corruption they know about e.g. bribery, vote buying, gift-giving, etc.
learners share personal or any known case of corruption.
in groups, learners discuss the causes and effects of corruption in society.
learners study a sample text on corruption and answer questions on it.
learner debate on the advantages and disadvantages of corruption e.g. “corruption is a necessary evil in society,” discuss.
learners brainstorm on the contribution they can make in fighting corruption.
learners brainstorm on ways of reducing corruption.
using relevant examples, teacher introduces noun classes 11-14.
teacher gives learners an exercise to identify more examples of nouns in classes 11-14.
using relevant examples, teacher introduces the concept of compounds.
learners do an exercise on compound nouns.

suggested_assessment_activities.description: in pairs, role-plays the benefits of grateful behaviour.
works in a group to write and perform a story/dialogue/ skit of dangers associated with unacceptable behaviour in a community.
writes from personal experience/ hearsay a composition on an example of a poor dress code that occurred in his/her locality.
researches and uses proverbs and sayings related to behaviours.
explains at least four types of corruption orally to other learners.
discusses the effects of corruption in a group.
in the same group, suggests ways of eradicating corruption.
writes an imaginative or expository composition on corruption.
in about 80-100 words summarises what happened in the video presentation on corruption.
reads and translates/ interprets into a local language a passage on corruption.
role play to demonstrate a corruption scene e.g in a public office, schools, roads etc.
write a report on a corruption incident he/she witnessed.
make/write a police statement giving evidence about a corruption incident witnessed.
reads a text and identifies compounded nouns.

suggested_uses: use a computer to prepare animations about a corruption scandal.
analyse a news item on corruption.

topics.core_competency: The learner understands vocabulary related to systems of governance.
learning_outcomes: comprehend leadership structures, qualities, types and values at different levels (u).
use noun classes 19 - 23 (where applicable) (k, u).
appreciate the values of elections and know the electoral processes (k, v, a).
state the types, roles and responsibilities of citizens (k, v, a).
use verb extensions 7- 9 (where applicable) (k, u).

suggested_learning_activities.description: learners identify the administrative hierarchy of their school and that of the prefects’ body.
teacher guides learners to identify the leadership structures of their country and traditional institution.
in groups, learners discuss qualities of a good leader citing relevant examples.
learners draw an organogram for any political or traditional institution.
using relevant examples, teacher introduces noun classes 19-23.
teacher gives learners an exercise to identify more examples of nouns in classes 19-23.
learners share their personal experiences of an electoral process they participated in e.g. local council or prefectoral election.
teacher guides learners to identify the stages involved in a local and national election.
learners brainstorm on qualifications or prerequisites for a voter e.g. age, id, citizenship, residence, etc.
in groups, learners write a one-page campaign speech for a public rally.
learners present their speeches in plenary.
learners debate on the values of elections e.g. “elections are of no value”; “democracy can only be realised through elections”.
learners brainstorm on the meaning and types of citizenship.
in groups, learners discuss their roles and responsibilities in their communities.
teacher helps to correlate their roles and responsibilities in their communities to the nation.
teacher guides learners to recap their understanding of verb conjugations.
using relevant examples, teacher illustrates verb conjugations 7-9 for example kola, kolera, kolakola, kolerera, koleka, kolesa, kozesa, kolagana, kolaganira.
in an exercise, teacher identifies verbs and asks learners to conjugate verbs in levels 7-9 (where applicable).

suggested_assessment_activities.description: in a group simulation exercise, dramatises a traditional/political leader gathering views on his/her roles as a representative of the electorate.
describes, in discussion and in writing, qualifications required of a voter and qualities of a good leader.
explains five electoral malpractices and suggests solutions.
administers a questionnaire or an interview guide to seek public opinion on elections.
uses the questionnaire in practice/ simulation.
identifies the roles of government and traditional leaders from texts/research and writes notes to deliver a short talk.
writes a campaign manifesto.
conducts campaigns in the classroom for the post of class monitor.
